chunks.text: SegWithU: Deterministic Perturbation Probes for Single-Backbone-Pass Risk-Aware Medical Image Segmentation Tianhao Fu 1, 4, 5, ⋆, Austin Wang †, 2, 5, Charles Chen †, 1, 5, Roby Aldave-Garza †, 3, 5, and Yucheng Chen 5 † Equal contributions. 1 University of Toronto, Toronto, ON, Canada 2 McGill University, Montreal, QC, Canada 3 University of Waterloo, Waterloo, ON, Canada 4 Vector Institute, Toronto, ON, Canada 5 Project Neura, Toronto, ON, Canada Abstract. Reliable uncertainty maps are needed when medical seg- mentations drive downstream measurements, triage, or clinical review. Strong uncertainty baselines often require repeated inference, while ef- ficient single-backbone-pass methods can be weak at ranking failures or depend on restrictive feature-space assumptions. We present SegWithU, a supervised frozen-backbone uncertainty module for medical image seg- mentation. SegWithU leaves a pretrained 3D segmentation backbone unchanged, taps decoder features, and learns a compact probe space whose deterministic signed perturbation patterns measure local predic- tion instability. The module produces two voxel-wise maps with dis- tinct roles: a calibration map for probability tempering and a ranking map for error localization and selective prediction. We explicitly formu- late the perturbation patterns, map dependencies, training losses, and voxel-level evaluation protocol. On ACDC, BraTS2024, and LiTS, Seg- WithU achieves AUROC/AURC of 0.9838/2.4885, 0.9946/0.2660, and 0.9925/0.8193, respectively, with AURC reported in 10−4 units, while preserving the frozen backbone’s hard segmentations. Ablations show that the calibration/ranking decomposition, ranking losses, and learned perturbation probes each contribute to performance. Code will be re- leased after review.

Keywords: Uncertainty estimation · Medical image segmentation · Se- lective prediction · Calibration · Risk coverage 1 Introduction Medical image segmentation is increasingly used as a quantitative instrument for anatomical measurement, lesion burden estimation, treatment planning, and longitudinal monitoring. Because plausible contours can still contain clinically ⋆Project lead with correspondence at tianhao.fu@mail.utoronto.ca. arXiv:2604.15271v4 [cs.CV] 18 Aug 2026 2 T. Fu, A. Wang, C. Chen, R. Garza, Y. Chen relevant errors, a deployed segmentor should expose not only what it predicts, but also where the prediction is unreliable. Uncertainty estimation is a natural reliability layer, but common methods trade accuracy, cost, and deployability. Deep ensembles, MC dropout, and test- time augmentation can be strong but require repeated inference or multiple mod- els [9,6,14]. ConfidNet instead learns to predict the true-class probability (TCP) as a surrogate for confidence, providing a lightweight learned confidence esti- mate but without optimizing uncertainty ranking or selective error detection [5]. Temperature scaling is efficient but mainly rescales confidence [8]. Deterministic methods such as DUQ, DUE, and DDU-Seg avoid repeated backbone passes, yet depend on feature geometry, density models, or training-time constraints that may be awkward for an already validated medical segmentor [1,10,11,12]. This deployment setting motivates SegWithU, a supervised uncertainty head attached to a frozen pretrained backbone. The operational premise is that un- reliable delineations should be unstable under small structured perturbations of tapped features. SegWithU learns a compact probe space, evaluates fixed deter- ministic signed perturbation patterns, and separates two uses of uncertainty: a positive calibration map that tempers logits for proper scoring rules and an un- constrained ranking map that orders voxels for selective prediction and review.

We explicitly define the probe patterns and use “single backbone pass” to mean one expensive frozen-backbone pass plus lightweight head computations. Our contributions are a frozen-backbone uncertainty module that preserves argmax segmentations, a deterministic perturbation-probe formulation with sep- arate calibration and ranking maps, voxel-level evaluation on three datasets, and ablations showing the importance of the two-map design, ranking losses, and learned probes. 2 Related Work Multi-pass uncertainty. Deep ensembles expose disagreement across indepen- dently trained models [9]; MC dropout retains dropout at test time [6]; and test-time augmentation measures variability under plausible input transforms [14]. They are useful references, but their cost scales with models, stochastic samples, or augmentations, which is especially relevant for volumetric images. Calibration and deterministic single-pass methods. Temperature scaling learns a global scalar temperature on validation data and can improve probability scores, but it does not optimize spatial error ranking [8]. ConfidNet learns a confidence predictor from intermediate features to regress the true-class probability (TCP), providing learned failure confidence without repeated stochastic inference [5]. DUQ and DUE use distance-aware deterministic representations [1,10], while DDU and DDU-Seg fit class-conditional feature densities [11,12]. These methods show that single-pass uncertainty or confidence estimation is possible, but rely on learned confidence regression, representation geometry, or high-dimensional density estimation. SegWithU for Risk-Aware Medical Segmentation 3 Fig. 1. Overview of SegWithU. A frozen segmentation backbone produces raw logits z and tapped decoder features h. A lightweight uncertainty head maps h to compact probe responses, evaluates deterministic signed perturbation patterns, and derives intermediate maps Uepi, Uprobe, Ures, and Uale.

These are combined with margin and entropy cues to produce Ucal for probability tempering and Urnk for voxel-wise error ranking. Positioning of SegWithU. Latent perturbation has precedents in adversarial ro- bustness, sensitivity analysis, and test-time perturbation methods [7,14]. Seg- WithU learns feature-tapped probe responses on a frozen backbone and uses finite deterministic perturbations to train two maps with different objectives, avoiding learned regression to a single confidence target, new constraints on global representation geometry, or class-conditional density fitting. 3 Method 3.1 Compact Formulation Let z = fθ(x) ∈RB×C×Ωbe frozen-backbone logits and let h be tapped decoder features after projection, resizing, concatenation, and fusion. In our DynUNet implementation, the taps come from two decoder upsampling blocks and the output block, giving both coarse semantic and finer boundary cues. SegWithU leaves z and the argmax mask unchanged. From h, a 1×1 head computes probes 4 T. Fu, A. Wang, C. Chen, R. Garza, Y. Chen v = ψ(h) ∈RB×R×Ωwith learned scales σr = softplus(αr) + ϵ. The full formula reference is provided in the supplementary appendix. 3.2 Calibration, Ranking, and Training Let p = softmax(z), margin m = p(1) −p(2), ambiguity weight w = exp(−γm) with default γ = 4, and Uale = softplus(ψale(h)).

The positive calibration map is Ucal = softplus{ψcal[log(1+Uepi +Ures), log(1+Uale), m]}, ˜z = z/ p 1 + Ucal, (3) so calibrated probabilities change but raw hard segmentations do not. Error localization uses an unconstrained score Urnk = (1 + 0.1 tanh(a))Uanchor + b + softplus(c)w, (4) where Uanchor = log(1 + Uepi) + 0.5 log(1 + Ures) + 0.25 log(1 + Ucal) + 0.25H(p)/ log C + w. Thus Ucal supports probabilistic scoring and Urnk ranks likely segmentation errors. The segmentation backbone is frozen and λseg = 0, so the uncertainty head cannot improve Dice by modifying masks. We optimize only the uncertainty head with L = 0.5LNLL + 0.25(LEC + LPairwise + LTail) + 0.05(LTrust + LAnchor + LResidual). (5) LNLL uses ˜z. Ranking losses use ui = Urnk,i and error labels ei = 1[ˆyi ̸= yi], with ˆyi = arg maxc zi,c. These include error-correlation BCE on standardized scores, an erroneous/correct pairwise margin, and a tail penalty for erroneous voxels assigned low uncertainty. Trust, anchor, and residual terms regularize perturbation magnitude, agreement with the anchor, and residual energy on easy voxels. SegWithU for Risk-Aware Medical Segmentation 5 4 Experiments 4.1 Datasets, Backbones, and Baselines We evaluate on ACDC cardiac MRI [2], BraTS2024 multimodal brain MRI [13], and LiTS abdominal CT [3]. Because BraTS2024 has no annotated public test set, we sample 200 training and 100 held-out test cases from the public training set; for LiTS, we reserve the final 10 cases for testing. These splits are not site-, scanner-, or vendor-held-out splits. All segmentation backbones are 3D DynUNet models trained on five non- overlapping folds plus one “all-data” model using MONAI tooling [4]. The five- fold Dice ranges were 88.21–90.51% on ACDC, 55.87–60.07% on BraTS2024, and 71.77–76.75% on LiTS. The corresponding all-data Dice scores were 90.35%, 62.75%, and 78.21%.

The BraTS Dice range frames the uncertainty comparison under this fixed-backbone protocol and should be considered when interpreting absolute mask quality. ACDC is resampled to a 64×128×128 patch because of coarse through-plane spacing; BraTS2024 and LiTS use 1283 patches. All backbones use Dice+CE training with 3D sliding-window inference and Gaussian blending. SegWithU trains only the second-stage uncertainty head with AdamW, cosine learning-rate scheduling, gradient clipping, early stopping, and the default R = K = 8 probe configuration. We compare SegWithU to Deep Ensembles, TTA, MC Dropout, TS, DUQ, DDU-Seg, DUE, and ConfidNet. Ranking uses each method’s native scalar un- certainty: ensemble mutual information; predictive-distribution uncertainty for MC Dropout and TTA; entropy after TS; native scores for DUQ, DDU-Seg, and DUE; and Urnk for SegWithU. For probabilistic scores, SegWithU uses probabil- ities tempered by Ucal; AUROC and AURC use Urnk and raw-logit hard errors. Calibration data. SegWithU trains a supervised second-stage uncertainty head on top of the frozen backbone. Our protocol uses the train/test separation above; in deployment, labeled validation data should be reserved for the uncertainty head and temperature-style baselines. 4.2 Voxel-Level Metrics Metrics are voxel-level over the test set. Let ˆyi = arg maxc zi,c and ei = 1[ˆyi ̸= yi]. Dice reports overlap; multi-class Brier is mean squared error between prob- abilities and one-hot labels; and AUROC tests whether uncertainty ui ranks erroneous voxels above correct voxels. For AURC, voxels are sorted from low to high uncertainty, the most confident α fraction is retained, and residual risk is Risk(α) = 1 ⌊αN⌋ ⌊αN⌋ X j=1 eπ(j). (6) AURC is the numerical area under this risk–coverage curve. Lower AURC is better, and all table values are reported in 10−4 units. 6 T. Fu, A. Wang, C. Chen, R. Garza, Y.

Multi-pass methods are high-cost references; the main comparison for SegWithU is the single-backbone-pass group. 4.3 Main Results Table 1 shows that SegWithU is the most consistent single-backbone-pass method for ranking uncertainty. It achieves the best AUROC and AURC on ACDC, BraTS2024, and LiTS while preserving the frozen-backbone Dice. On ACDC, SegWithU improves AURC over DUE by 17.7% (3.0233 to 2.4885) and slightly over Deep Ensembles (2.5326 to 2.4885), despite using one backbone pass rather than five models. On BraTS2024, it improves AURC over DUE by 9.9% and over TTA by 14.4%, while matching the all-data backbone Dice. On LiTS, it gives the lowest AURC (0.8193) and highest AUROC (0.9925), although DUE has the best Dice and Brier. The main gain is stronger voxel ordering for selective prediction, while segmentation quality and calibration remain tied to the frozen backbone and calibration map. Multi-pass baselines remain important references and are sometimes competitive, but require repeated inference; on BraTS2024, Deep Ensembles also inherit weaker fold-specific backbones. 4.4 Qualitative Analysis Figure 2 shows that SegWithU tends to attach high uncertainty to anatomical boundaries and failure regions rather than diffuse background. Table 2 gives the corresponding case metrics for the displayed DE/DUQ/DUE/SegWithU com- parison. On ACDC case 7, Deep Ensembles produce a broad halo and DUQ in- troduces isolated high-uncertainty components away from the contour, whereas SegWithU keeps uncertainty closer to the cardiac contour and is best on all four metrics. On BraTS2024 case 44, the lesion is irregular and all methods have limited Dice, but SegWithU places uncertainty near the lesion boundary, gives the best Dice, and remains close to DUQ/DUE on ranking. On LiTS case 8, all methods show liver-boundary uncertainty; SegWithU produces fewer isolated high-uncertainty regions away from the liver and lesion, emphasizes the lesion region, and is best on Dice/AUROC/AURC while remaining close to the best Brier value. 4.5 Statistical Testing and Significance Scoring Case-wise paired two-sided Wilcoxon tests compare methods within each dataset–metric family. p-values are Holm-corrected over all pairwise method tests; α = 0.05. Directions follow the metric: higher Dice/AUROC and lower Brier/AURC are better. Because the backbone is frozen, Dice remains 0.9035±0.0044 for all variants. Calibration and ranking should be separated: calibration-only keeps Brier competitive at 0.0114 but collapses AUROC/AURC to 0.7078/28.0538, while ranking-only recovers 0.9824/2.9853 but worsens Brier to 0.0122. Rank- ing losses are central. Removing NLL, error-correlation, pairwise, tail, and trust terms gives AURC 4.4299, 4.5017, 16.7523, 3.4856, and 2.7331, respectively, com- pared with 2.4885 for the full model. The pairwise term is especially important, dropping AUROC from 0.9838 to 0.9275 when removed. Finally, SegWithU ab- lations using a direct uncertainty head, fixed perturbation scales, or removing the aleatoric branch yield AURC 4.0557, 3.0440, and 4.8666, respectively. These drops indicate that the learned perturbation-probe mechanism contributes be- yond a generic auxiliary uncertainty head. Off-diagonal entries compare row and column methods across test cases; the matrix is symmetric, and ≪denotes p < 0.0001. 4.7 Efficiency and Selective-Prediction Behavior SegWithU adds about 0.1M parameters and preserves single-backbone-pass inference. Measured wall-clock times for SegWithU are 0.23/0.54/14.46 s on ACDC/BraTS2024/LiTS, compared with 1.72/2.63/39.48 s for Deep Ensembles, 0.50/1.18/31.31 s for TTA, 1.25/2.96/90.38 s for MC Dropout, 0.92/3.24/45.52 s for DUE, and 1.59/4.79/60.97 s for ConfidNet. Thus the main comparison is not only accuracy but whether a lightweight add-on can recover much of the ranking quality of expensive uncertainty references. The risk–coverage examples in the supplement show that SegWithU is usually in the favorable low-risk group as uncertain voxels are rejected, although the leading curve can vary by case and coverage level. In the accuracy-threshold plots, retained voxels generally become more accurate as the confidence cutoff increases. This supports selective acceptance and targeted review, rather than treating uncertainty only as a scalar calibration diagnostic. 5 Discussion and Limitations SegWithU adds supervised reliability estimation to a frozen segmentor without changing hard predictions or rerunning the heavy 3D backbone.

We evaluate public benchmarks rather than held-out site, scanner, vendor, or protocol shifts. BraTS2024 and LiTS are multi-institutional or multi-center datasets, and ACDC includes disease-group and acquisition variation, but our splits do not isolate those factors. SegWithU also requires labeled data for the un- certainty head, so deployment should reserve a calibration/validation set. Within this scope, SegWithU combines frozen-backbone deployment, explicit calibra- tion/ranking separation, and direct voxel-wise risk-ordering losses. Here BCE denotes BCEWithLogits. B. Experimental Protocol Datasets and splits. ACDC: 3D cardiac MRI, 4 classes, official 200/100 train/test split, resampled, patch 64×128×128. BraTS2024: 4-channel brain MRI, 5 classes, 200 train and 100 held-out cases sampled from the public training set, patch 1283. LiTS: abdominal CT, 3 classes, fi- nal 10 cases held out, patch 1283. Foreground patches are oversampled at 33%. ACDC is resampled because through-plane spacing is coarse; BraTS and LiTS use no spacing alignment in the reported implementation. All datasets use dataset-specific intensity normalization. Backbones and inference. All backbones are 3D DynUNet models trained on five non-overlapping folds plus an all-data model.

Fold/all Dice: ACDC 88.21–90.51/90.35%; BraTS2024 55.87–60.07/62.75%; LiTS 71.77– 76.75/78.21%. Backbone training uses Dice+CE, SGD momentum 0.9, LR 0.01, polynomial decay p = 0.9, batch sizes 16/8/8, and 200 epochs. All 3D inference uses sliding windows with Gaussian blending, overlap 0.5, window batch size 2, and the dataset ROI above. Baselines. Deep Ensembles average the five fold backbones and score un- certainty from predictive-distribution mutual information. TTA uses the 8 axis-aligned 3D flip combinations, inverse-flips logits, averages probabil- ities, and scores entropy/variance. MC Dropout enables only dropout at inference on a dropout-enabled DynUNet and averages repeated stochastic sliding-window predictions. Temperature Scaling fits one scalar tempera- ture on validation data by NLL; fitted temperatures are close to 1.5, and entropy of tempered probabilities is the ranking score. DUQ uses BCE plus gradient penalty λ = 0.5, SGD momentum 0.9, LR 0.05, MultiStep decay, centroid size 8, length scale 0.1, and EMA γ = 0.999. DDU-Seg trains Dice+CE, then fits class-conditional Gaussian densities on penultimate features using streaming Chan covariance estimates. DUE uses an SVGP head with RBF kernel, M = 16 inducing points for ACDC and M = 64 for BraTS/LiTS, K-means initialization, auxiliary CE weight 0.5, spectral normalization, 32 posterior samples per spatial location, and spatial sub- sampling to 32,768 locations per step. ConfidNet learns a confidence head that regresses the model’s true-class probability (TCP) from intermediate features of the DynUNet. SegWithU implementation. SegWithU trains only a frozen-backbone uncertainty head. Multi-scale taps are upsamples.1.conv_block, upsamples.2.conv_block, and output_block, with channels (256, 128, 32) fused to 32 channels. Default probes use R = K = 8, σinit = 0.1, margin weight γ = 4, and the aleatoric branch enabled.

Optimization uses AdamW, LR 10−3, β = (0.9, 0.999), ϵ = 10−8, cosine annealing to 3×10−4, gradient clipping at 12, up to 200 epochs, early-stopping tolerance 10, and no deep supervision. Loss weights are λnll = 0.5, λec = λpair = λtail = 0.25, λtrust = λanchor = λres = 0.05, and λseg = 0. Evaluation details. Ranking maps are: ensemble mutual information for Deep Ensembles; predictive entropy for MC Dropout, TTA, and TS; na- tive aleatoric/deterministic scores for DUQ, DDU-Seg, and DUE; Urnk for SegWithU. 1−[ TCP for ConfidNet, where its auxiliary confidence head ap- proximates the voxel-wise true-class probability. SegWithU uses Ucal only for probability tempering in Brier/NLL-style scores. AURC sorts voxels by increasing uncertainty and numerically integrates risk–coverage; risk– coverage plots also use random-rejection and oracle references. Accuracy- threshold plots use 101 thresholds on [0, 1]. Comparison caveats. DUQ, DDU, and DUE were originally classifi- cation methods; dense segmentation treats voxels as conditionally inde- pendent samples and changes computational scaling. ConfidNet has an optional stage that fine-tunes a copy of the segmentation model after training the confidence network. We omit this fine-tuning stage to main- tain the same frozen-backbone constraint as SegWithU; additionally, in our experiments, the fine-tuned variant did not improve any metric on ACDC, BraTS, or LiTS compared to the original. Original baselines did not use MONAI DynUNet, so absolute values may differ from their pa- pers. DUQ hyperparameters were inherited from low-resolution classifica- tion; Deep Ensembles omit adversarial training; MC Dropout depends on where dropout appears in DynUNet; DUE inference is stochastic unless the GP sampling seed is fixed.
